transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-10-29 15:00 UTC | Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Rourke (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (BrightRoute Lead Backend), Tom Reyes (PM), Dr. Mei Huang (BrightRoute ML)
---
[00:00:05] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining i think we'll give about 40 minutes today we're gonna walk through a quick sandbox demo of hosted chat gen, show streaming behavior, how params affect latency/cost, and then cover retries and idempotency patterns. quick intros — why don't you folks say hi?
[00:00:20] Aisha: hi i'm aisha lead backend at brightroute we own the in-app assistant service and want to understand how streaming will work with our websocket proxy and also the retry story because we have strict idempotency requirements for billing-related flows
[00:00:32] Tom: tom here product — timeline is pilot in 3 weeks if feasibility looks good from infra/security
[00:00:36] Dr. Mei: mei, ml eng, i'll bring sample prompts and eval sets. i'm curious about partial outputs and how to resume if stream cuts out
[00:00:44] Liam: great thanks, i'll be demoing the console and some code snippets. quick note, i'll refer to Redwood's hosted model variants — sometimes the transcribe stuffs calls them redwood-lite or rwd-large in our slides, so excuse small naming slips
[00:00:58] Maya: ok jumping in, first a live sandbox in the console. (brief pause, typing) 
[00:01:10] Liam: so here's the playground — you can open a streaming session with the chat endpoint, and you'll see tokens come back incrementally. for your use case with websockets you likely want to stream to the client with chunking: we recommend 50-200ms flush windows for typing-like UX.
[00:01:35] Tom: 50 to 200 ms, ok that seems tight. what's the throughput impact?
[00:01:38] Liam: more frequent flushes increase number of messages but not tokens; overhead is mostly network round trips. typically cost is unaffected but latency perception improves. if you need to optimize, increase flush batch or rely on prefix caching.
[00:01:53] Aisha: you said prefix caching — is that the built-in KV cache or do we have to manage redis?
[00:01:58] Liam: good question — Redwood has an automatic prefix/KV cache in the runtime that stores repeated prompt prefixes and KV entries (we sometimes see notes calling it K V cache), that reduces compute for repeated context. you can also use your external store — many teams keep a hot redis for conversation metadata and then rely on Redwood's runtime for token cache.
[00:02:18] Dr. Mei: if i resume a partial stream after a disconnect does the model resume generating mid-token or restart?
[00:02:23] Liam: by default, on a reconnect you push the conversation state and the runtime will resume from the last cached KV slot. if the stream cut mid-token you might get a slightly different continuation, so we recommend an idempotent resume: maintain a client-side sequence id and on reconnect send the last acknowledged token index. Redwood also supports server-side resumptions for many model variants — but there are edge cases when quantized models behave differently.
[00:02:48] Tom: that sounds important — can you show retry logic?
[00:02:51] Liam: sure. here's a simple pseudocode pattern: attach an idempotency key to the session request, set exponential backoff and a max attempts, and on failure check whether partial output was delivered — if yes, ask runtime for delta via the conversation cursor. (typing) the console shows headers like x-redwood-idempotency and a conversation-cursor field.
[00:03:15] Maya: some customers call these headers by other names, i've seen proxies strip them out, so check your gateway. aisha, do you run a gateway that modifies headers?
[00:03:23] Aisha: yes we have an edge proxy that rewrites a few headers for security — we'll need a note on the header names and whether they can be placed in body instead
[00:03:29] Liam: we can put idemp keys in the JSON body as well; we'll share a snippet. also note the retry semantics are idempotent for generation requests if idempotency key is present, but for streaming we recommend the resume flow: client sends last token ack and the runtime responds with the remaining continuation.
[00:03:48] Tom: what about status codes? how do we differentiate between transient 5xx and permanent errors?
[00:03:52] Liam: 5xx are usually transient — our SDKs classify most 5xx as retryable with capped backoff. 4xx like input-too-large or unauthorized are permanent. console docs show a mapping. we also surface a retryable boolean in the JSON error payload in many cases.
[00:04:07] Dr. Mei: can you talk about token accounting and partial responses? if a stream disconnects and i re-request, will we pay twice for overlapping tokens?
[00:04:15] Liam: good point — for hosted usage we bill per token observed by the runtime; when you resume with an idempotency key and cursor, the runtime avoids double charging for tokens included in the previous session. if you simply re-send a full prompt without idemp, yes you'll be billed again. we recommend conversations with cursors or server-side caching.
[00:04:34] Aisha: what's the cost delta between streaming to client frequently vs aggregating and sending a single message?
[00:04:39] Liam: cost is primarily model compute per token; network messages don't change token count. but smaller flush windows increase latency to final token (you get partials earlier), and slight overhead on connection churn but not large. Optimize can recommend flush windows by measuring per-request latencies.
[00:04:58] Maya: quick detour — security: BrightRoute asked about SOC2 and KMS. we have SOC2 docs and customers can integrate KMS for key management in Private/Dedicated. since you're evaluating hosted first, you can use our customer-managed KMS via our private offering later.
[00:05:15] Tom: perfect, please send.
[00:05:18] Liam: back to demo — here's a live trace in the console: you can see per-token latencies and a token-level cost estimate. (noise, typing) you can toggle model variant: rwd-large-8bit, rwd-medium, etc — smaller variants drop latency and cost but might reduce quality on long-context prompts.
[00:05:40] Dr. Mei: do you support custom quantization profiles? we run long context 16k prompts often
[00:05:45] Liam: yes we have quantization and compilation profiles; Optimize recommends quant/sequence length pairs. for 16k we often use a medium quant with dedicated GPU pools. when in hosted you can pin a model version and we can recommend kernel selection.
[00:06:00] Aisha: we have peaky load — 200 concurrent users during peak. what's the recommended pattern?
[00:06:04] Liam: for peaks we recommend a mix: use hosted for baseline and burst to Dedicated or use auto-burst policies. Also use prefix caching to reduce compute on repeated flows. Redwood's autoscaling and burst routing can route by cost policy so you keep latency SLOs.
[00:06:22] Tom: can you show a failure-mode example — a websocket drop and a client reconnect?
[00:06:26] Liam: yep — demoing now. (simulated disconnect) you see the client reconnect sends conversation-cursor: 'c-983' and idempotency: 'br-20251029-01' and runtime resumes at token 124. small stutter but final result consistent.
[00:06:45] Aisha: nice — on our side we need deterministic outputs for billing messages. is there a guarantee about exact same output on resume?
[00:06:52] Liam: exact bit-for-bit replay is not guaranteed in all cases, especially across quantized variants and kernel changes. but with a pinned model version and cursor, you get deterministic enough behavior for most flows. for strict determinism, export the generated text to your store once confirmed, and use that canonical result for billing.
[00:07:10] Tom: how long does a conversation-cursor persist?
[00:07:13] Liam: default is 24 hours for hosted but can be configured for Dedicated/Private to longer retention. we can extend for pilots if you need.
[00:07:21] Dr. Mei: any gotchas for streaming with low-latency mobile clients?
[00:07:25] Liam: mobile clients need jitter buffers and to honor chunk order; we recommend websocket pings and an ack window. also avoid too-large initial prompts to minimize warmup. if you have cold starts, Optimize can suggest pre-warming strategies.
[00:07:40] Maya: ok quick walkthrough of the Optimize tab — it suggests batching profiles, quantization recommendations, and per-route latency/cost tradeoffs. you can upload traffic samples and it will simulate cost across model variants.
[00:07:55] Aisha: that's useful — can you run our sample after we share it?
[00:07:58] Liam: yes we'll run three scenarios: conversational chat, ticket summarize, and short Q/A. we'll push results to the shared spreadsheet.
[00:08:05] Tom: what about SDKs for reconnect logic?
[00:08:08] Liam: our SDKs include helpers for streaming ack, idempotency keys, and auto resumes. example in node/python snippets in the console. we'll attach a ready-to-run snippet to the follow-up.
[00:08:20] Maya: any questions on pricing? brief note: hosted is usage-based; Dedicated is reserved capacity. i'll send a pricing note tailored to your expected token volume based on the Optimize run.
[00:08:32] Aisha: minor question — if we do a short pilot on hosted and then move to Dedicated, how seamless is the migration?
[00:08:37] Liam: seamless — same API and console. you can pin model versions and route by policy. we also provide migration docs and a network checklist for VPC/private options.
[00:08:50] Tom: ok wrap up then next steps?
[00:08:53] Maya: recap: we'll share sandbox quickstart + code snippets, Liam will run the Optimize runs on your 48h sample, Aisha to share traffic and prompts, Maya to send SOC2 and KMS notes and pricing. schedule pilot cluster next week — do we agree?
[00:09:08] Aisha: yes agree.
[00:09:10] Tom: yes.
[00:09:12] Dr. Mei: sounds good — also, Liam can you include the retry matrix and example idempotency header names?
[00:09:18] Liam: will do.
[00:09:20] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with artifacts. end of call.
---
Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels (typical), a couple of model names abbreviated in the console. Some words (K V vs KV) are spelled out in the recording.
